Spousal and child support and tax in 2026: what the payer deducts, what the recipient reports, and why child support is paid first

A worked guide to the federal tax treatment of support under a court order or written agreement made after April 1997: why child support is neither deductible nor taxable, when spousal support goes on lines 22000 and 12800, the priority rule that turns a short payment into lost deductions, lump sums and third-party payments, the year-of-separation choice against line 30400, the effect on RRSP room, and CRA statistics on who deducts support. Six charts and an editable model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 11 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Split a year’s support payments into child and spousal support and see the 2026 federal tax on each side

Original illustration of the 2026 federal tax treatment of support paid under a court order or written agreement made after April 1997. Child support is neither deductible by the payer nor taxable to the recipient. Spousal support stated separately in the order is deducted by the payer on line 22000 and included by the recipient on line 12800, but only once all child support owed for the year and earlier years is paid, because each year’s payments count first as child support. Federal tax uses the 2026 brackets and the 14% basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered; provincial tax, other credits and income-tested benefits are not included. The year-of-separation option compares the deduction with a line 30400 claim for a child with no income. The model assumes the payments are periodic, the recipient can use them as they see fit and the order is registered where required; it does not model pre-May 1997 orders, lump sums, third-party payments or the T1157 election.

The central idea

Under orders and agreements made after April 1997, child support is paid from the payer’s after-tax income and arrives tax-free. Spousal support stated separately in the order is deductible by the payer on line 22000 and taxable to the recipient on line 12800, but each year’s payments count first as child support, so a payer who falls behind loses the spousal deduction until all child support is caught up. The deduction is worth the payer’s marginal rate and the tax is the recipient’s, so the net federal effect depends on the gap between their two brackets.

01

Two kinds of support, two tax results

When a couple separates, an order or agreement usually sets two kinds of payments. The tax rules treat them in opposite ways:

Federal treatment of support under an order or agreement made after April 1997
Child supportSpousal or common-law partner support
PayerNot deductible; paid from after-tax incomeDeductible on line 22000, if the conditions are met
RecipientNot taxableTaxable on line 12800
Reported in totalLine 21999 (payer) and line 12799 (recipient)Line 21999 and line 12799, then the taxable or deductible part on lines 22000 and 12800
Effect on net incomeNone for either personLowers the payer’s net income and raises the recipient’s

Under Folio S1-F3-C3 (¶3.13), any amount the order does not identify as solely for the spouse or former spouse is a child support amount. A single global figure “for the family” is therefore treated entirely as child support, with no deduction. Spousal support has to be stated separately to be deductible.

The date matters because orders made before May 1997 followed the older rule, under which child support was deductible and taxable too. Such an order moves to the current rules if the child support is changed after April 1997, if a new order between the same people changes the total, if the order names a date from which the new rules apply, or if both parties sign Form T1157. The election cannot be reversed. This guide models current-rule orders only.

02

When spousal support is deductible

Under the Income Tax Act definition of a support amount (subsection 56.1(4)), as CRA explains it in the Folio, a payment is deductible to the payer and taxable to the recipient only if all of these apply:

  • It is paid under a court order or written agreement. A written agreement is generally signed and dated by both parties; emails alone may not be enough (¶3.31). Registering the order or agreement with CRA is required to claim the deduction.
  • It is an allowance payable on a periodic basis: a set amount fixed in advance and paid, for example, monthly. Payments at intervals of more than a year, or a sum for a fixed term that looks like a property settlement, may not qualify (¶3.38–3.43).
  • The recipient can use it as they see fit. Payments to third parties are covered below.
  • The two people were living separate and apart because of the breakdown of the relationship when the payment was made. Spouses are treated as separated only after 90 consecutive days apart (¶3.7–3.9).
  • Payments made before the order or agreement count only if made in the same or the preceding year and the document says they are considered paid under it (subsections 60.1(3) and 56.1(3)).

Amounts paid on top of what the order requires, such as gifts or pocket money sent directly to children, are not support and are left off lines 21999 and 12799. Legal fees to obtain a separation or divorce are not deductible by either person. A recipient may deduct fees to collect overdue support or to establish or increase it on line 22100. Interest on arrears is not deductible by the payer but must be included by the recipient (¶3.65).

03

A worked year

Take a former couple with an order made in 2025. The payer has CAD 110,000 of employment income; the recipient has CAD 35,000 and the children. The order requires CAD 1,000 a month of child support and CAD 1,500 a month of spousal support, and the payer pays all CAD 30,000 in 2026.

Default case in the model, 2026 federal tax
ItemPayerRecipient
Total paid or received (line 21999 / 12799)CAD 30,000CAD 30,000
Child support, not deductible or taxableCAD 12,000CAD 12,000
Spousal support (line 22000 / 12800)CAD 18,000 deductedCAD 18,000 included
Net income after supportCAD 92,000CAD 53,000
Federal tax effectCAD 3,690 saved (20.5% bracket)CAD 2,520 added (14% bracket)
After federal taxCost CAD 26,310Kept CAD 27,480

The CAD 18,000 deduction stays within the payer’s 20.5% band (CAD 58,523 to 117,045), and the inclusion stays within the recipient’s 14% band, so the two federal returns together pay CAD 1,170 less than if the spousal support were not deductible. Provincial tax adds a similar effect at provincial rates. The first chart shows how the saving and the added tax change with the amount: each moves at the marginal rate of the person concerned, so the net effect shrinks or reverses when the recipient has the higher income or the support pushes them into a higher bracket.

Family law usually takes this into account. The Federal Child Support Guidelines set child support from the payer’s income on the basis that it is not deductible, and the Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines are expressed in gross, pre-tax amounts that assume deductibility. This guide does not calculate how much support is owed.

04

The priority rule: short payments are child support first

If the order sets both kinds of support, CRA treats every payment in a year as child support until all child support for that year and earlier years is paid. Only payments above that count as spousal support and can be deducted. Under the paragraph 60(b) formula, the Folio shows the shortfall reducing the deduction dollar for dollar (Example 1).

With the CAD 30,000 owed in the default case:

  • a payer who pays CAD 24,000 has paid all CAD 12,000 of child support and CAD 12,000 of spousal support; the deduction is CAD 12,000, saving CAD 2,460 instead of CAD 3,690;
  • a payer who pays CAD 10,000 has paid only child support, deducts nothing, and owes CAD 2,000 of child support that is added to the next year’s child support before any spousal support can be deducted again;
  • a payer with child support arrears from earlier years must clear them first in the same way.

The rule applies separately to each recipient: arrears owed to one former partner do not cut the deduction for support paid to another (Folio Example 4). It does not apply where child and spousal support are under different orders with different recipients. CRA’s page on the amount to claim or report includes an example where a payer who stopped paying after three months cannot deduct any spousal support, while the recipient is still shown as reporting the spousal part of what was paid. The model applies the Folio’s formula to both returns, so if a real case has a shortfall, check the treatment with CRA or a tax professional.

05

Lump sums, retroactive payments and third-party payments

  • Lump sums are generally not periodic and so not deductible or taxable, especially a sum paid to settle future obligations or released rights. Exceptions are arrears of periodic amounts that fell due after the order or agreement, an advance of future periodic support under a court order, and retroactive periodic support for a period before a court order. A lump sum under a written agreement for a period before that agreement does not qualify (Folio ¶3.44–3.46). A recipient of a qualifying retroactive lump sum of CAD 3,000 or more may be able to ask CRA to tax it as if received in the earlier years (Form T1198).
  • Payments to third parties, such as rent, a mortgage or medical bills paid directly, are deemed paid to the recipient (subsection 60.1(1)) but still need to be a support amount. For specific-purpose payments to count, the order or agreement must say that subsections 60.1(2) and 56.1(2) apply, or clearly state they are taxable to the recipient and deductible by the payer. Payments for a home the payer lives in are excluded, and payments toward buying or improving the recipient’s home are limited to 20% of the original loan principal each year (¶3.50–3.61).
  • Repaid support: a recipient who repays support under a court order that they earlier reported can deduct the repayment on line 22000 in the year of repayment or either of the two following years.

06

The year of separation: deduction or line 30400

A payer generally cannot claim the amount for an eligible dependant (line 30400) for a child they must pay support for. In the year a couple separates, though, a payer who meets the line 30400 conditions for the child, for example because the child lived with them before the separation, can choose: deduct the spousal support paid on line 22000, or enter zero there and claim the personal credits (line 30400 and, for that child, lines 30425 and 31800). They cannot have both for the same year.

The line 30400 credit for a child with no income is CAD 16,452 at 14%, or CAD 2,303.28. The deduction is worth the payer’s marginal federal rate on the spousal support paid. At CAD 110,000 of income, that is 20.5% until the deduction carries the payer below CAD 58,523, so the deduction wins once spousal support passes about CAD 11,235. A payer paying CAD 8,000 of spousal support would save CAD 1,640 by deducting it and CAD 2,303.28 with the credit. The choice affects only the payer’s return: the recipient still includes the spousal support. The fifth chart shows the crossover for the incomes entered; provincial credits and rates change it in practice.

07

Knock-on effects: RRSP room and income-tested benefits

  • RRSP room. Earned income for RRSP purposes adds taxable support received and subtracts deductible support paid. In the default case, the recipient’s 2027 RRSP room rises by CAD 3,240 (18% of CAD 18,000) and the payer’s falls by the same amount, both subject to the annual dollar limit and each person’s other earned income.
  • Benefits based on net income. Taxable spousal support raises the recipient’s net income, which is the starting point for the Canada child benefit, the GST/HST credit and many provincial benefits paid from July of the following year. Deductible support lowers the payer’s net income. For a recipient in a benefit phase-out range, the after-tax and after-benefit value of each dollar of spousal support is lower than the tax calculation alone shows. Child support does not count as income for these benefits.
  • Instalments. No tax is withheld from support payments. A recipient whose taxable support is large relative to tax withheld from other income may owe a balance at filing and may be asked to pay instalments.

08

Who deducts support: CRA statistics

CRA’s final statistics for the 2024 tax year (data as of 30 November 2025) show 51,360 returns deducting support payments made, for CAD 1.12 billion, about CAD 21,884 each. These are deductible amounts, mostly spousal support under current-rule orders, plus support under older orders that never moved to the new rules; child support paid under current orders does not appear.

09

Checklist and limits of the model

  • Find the date of the order or agreement and any later change: current rules apply from May 1997 or the change.
  • Check that spousal support is stated as a separate amount; an undivided amount is child support.
  • Register the order or agreement with CRA if you will deduct spousal support.
  • Keep records of every payment, date and recipient; both people report the total on line 21999 or 12799.
  • Pay child support for the year and any arrears in full before counting anything as deductible spousal support.
  • Check third-party payment clauses and any lump sum against the Folio before deducting or excluding them.
  • In the year of separation, compare the deduction with the line 30400 credit for the child.
  • Recipients: plan for the tax on spousal support, possible instalments and the effect on next year’s benefits.

The model uses 2026 federal brackets and treats net income as taxable income, with the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered. It assumes an order made after April 1997, periodic payments the recipient controls, one recipient, and that the CRA registration and living-apart conditions are met. Provincial and territorial tax, other credits, income-tested benefits and Quebec’s separate system are not included, and it does not decide how much support is owed. Use tax software, a family lawyer or a tax professional for an actual case.
